Neurology · published research

Facial nerve injury

Most rat and mouse studies report improved axonal regeneration or faster facial-movement recovery with PBM, while one wavelength comparison found benefit at 633 nm but not at 804 nm. No direct clinical facial-nerve injury study was identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Most rat and mouse studies report improved axonal regeneration or faster facial-movement recovery with PBM, while one wavelength comparison found benefit at 633 nm but not at 804 nm. No direct clinical facial-nerve injury study was identified.

Summary of the Evidence

The two facial-nerve categories contain 13 unique publications, all animal studies: twelve rat reports and one mouse report. Several articles arise from repeated experimental programs on nerve suturing or repair with a heterologous fibrin biopolymer. These are publication counts, not 13 verified independent laboratories or necessarily 13 distinct repair cohorts.

Human and clinical evidence

No direct study in people with facial nerve injury was identified. The database contains no clinical trial, patient series or clinical protocol for this indication.

Animal evidence

Most reports examine nerve section, crush or surgical repair and measure facial movement, axon structure or muscle recovery. Lee et al. found faster functional recovery and favorable nerve measures in rats treated at 633 nm, while 804-nm treatment did not show the same positive findings (Lee et al. 2021). A mouse study after facial-nerve section and suture reported faster whisker movement recovery with LED PBM than control (Er-Rouassi et al. 2022). Several rat studies using fibrin sealant plus PBM report better morphologic or functional repair than untreated injury, while another study found no statistically significant differences on several nerve measures. Combinations with biomaterials or other agents cannot establish the effect of PBM alone.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified in the two facial-nerve categories. Tissue markers and histology were measured in the animal experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Studies use red visible wavelengths such as 633 nm and near-infrared wavelengths around 804 or 808 nm, usually applied locally over the injured nerve or repair site. Some use LEDs and others laser devices. Treatment is often paired with microsurgical repair or a fibrin material. Power, exposure, frequency and follow-up vary across reports, so their findings do not define one transferable clinical protocol.

Interpretation

The animal literature supports continued testing of PBM as an adjunct to peripheral nerve repair, with outcomes depending on wavelength and repair context. It does not establish clinical effectiveness, and the frequent use of surgical or biomaterial combinations leaves the independent contribution of light uncertain.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for facial nerve recovery in people because the mapped evidence is entirely preclinical. Low within animal models for improved early functional recovery because most reports favor PBM but wavelengths and repair methods differ.
Publications and records13 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Thirteen animal publications report nerve or facial-muscle outcomes, but there are no direct human injury studies. Several reports combine PBM with nerve-repair procedures or fibrin biomaterials, and some wavelengths produced no clear benefit. Human trials should distinguish PBM alone from repair adjuncts and measure facial function over time.
